text: With the new config key naming a valid version-1 rule-set file and a MySQL `database.url`, `sqllens validate` exits 0 and `sqllens serve` starts.

A rule-set file with an unknown field in any record, a missing required field, a wrong-typed value (a Boolean where a number is expected, a TOML date for `generated_on` and a `role_id` other than its set's `name` included), an ID with a leading zero or a non-digit, an identifier outside `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`, a duplicate set or table name, a duplicate entry in any list (`columns = ["id", "name", "id"]` included), a predicate column also listed in `columns`, `metadata` key names that are not three distinct identifiers, or a `metadata` key name that SQL Lens reserves (`starter_ui_request`, `ui_features_available`) makes `sqllens validate` exit 2 and `sqllens serve` refuse to start, and the error names the record and the problem (at minimum these cases).
A rule-set file whose `source` records hold only `confirmed_against_production` loads, and a file whose `source` records hold every provenance field the version-1 format defines loads unchanged.

`sqllens validate` exits 2 and `sqllens serve` refuses to start, each with a message naming the cause, for a rule-set file that holds a `row_rule` (the message saying to remove the whole rule set, never only its row rules), for a non-MySQL `database.url`, and for a `binding.database` that differs from the database named in `database.url`, even when it equals `[database] name`.

For a rule-set file with unconfirmed sets, `sqllens validate` exits 0 and prints one `Warning:` line naming each unconfirmed set, and `sqllens serve` starts and logs one warning naming each unconfirmed set.

With a listed table or listed column missing from the connected MySQL database, a listed name whose letter case differs from the database's, or a listed table that is a view, `sqllens serve` (preflight on) refuses to start and `sqllens validate --check-db` exits 2, each naming the mismatched table or column.

With `--no-preflight` and a listed column missing from the database, every rule-set request that passes the five request classes and the conversation-owner check is refused with `isError` before the agent runs, with text saying the rule-set file could not be confirmed against the database and naming no table or column. The server log names the missing column, and once the column exists the next such request is served. A request that also fails one of the five request classes is refused as that class.

Each of exactly these five request classes is refused with `isError: true` before the agent runs, with text naming the class and no `_meta` value: rule-set key missing or empty; rule-set name not a string or whole number or naming no set; account key missing or its decimal text not in `binding.account_ids`; user key missing or not a positive whole number; the named set unconfirmed.

A rule-set name sent as the number `2` or the string `"2"` selects set `"2"`, while `"02"`, `2.0`, `true`, `null`, `[2]` and `{}` are refused as naming no set. A user ID sent as `7`, `"7"` or `"007"` is accepted as 7, while `0`, `-1`, `"7a"`, `true` and `7.0` are refused as an invalid user ID.
A request whose `_meta` has more than 64 keys is refused as rule-set key missing.

Under the example set, each of these runs and returns rows: `SELECT c.name, o.total FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`; `SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders ORDER BY n`; `SELECT c.name AS nm FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY nm`; `SELECT name FROM customers UNION SELECT name FROM customers ORDER BY name`; `WITH t AS (SELECT c.name AS nm FROM customers c) SELECT t.nm FROM t`; `SELECT d.n FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders o) d`; `SELECT name, total FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`; `SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)`; `SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id)`; `SELECT o.customer_id AS cust, SUM(o.total) AS revenue FROM orders o GROUP BY cust HAVING revenue > 100`; and `SELECT NAME FROM customers`. `SELECT name FROM CUSTOMERS` is refused.

Under the example set, a statement that reads `customers.email`, `orders.discount` or the predicate column `customers.rep_id` fails with MySQL's unknown-column error (1054) and returns no value of that column, exactly as `customers.nosuch` does. At minimum these placements of `customers.email` fail this way: the select list, `WHERE`, `JOIN … ON`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING MAX(customers.email) > ''`, an `ORDER BY` expression, a window `ORDER BY`, a function argument, `customers JOIN orders USING (email)`, a correlated reference from an `EXISTS` subquery, and `SELECT (SELECT x FROM (SELECT email AS x) d) FROM customers`. A statement that reads `salaries` is refused before execution.

Under the example set, `SELECT o.total AS discount, COUNT(*) FROM orders o GROUP BY discount` groups by `o.total` and returns no value of `orders.discount`. With `database.refuse_whole_row_selects = false`, `SELECT * FROM customers` and `SELECT c.* FROM customers c` return only `id` and `name`.

With no `[[rls]]` rules, the example set selected and the MySQL server's global `sql_mode` set to `ANSI`, `SELECT "email" FROM customers` returns the string `email` in every row, never a value of `customers.email`, and `SELECT name || '-' AS v FROM customers WHERE id = 1` returns the value it returns on a server in MySQL's default `sql_mode`. With `HIGH_NOT_PRECEDENCE` set, `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE name IS NOT NULL` returns the number of customers that have a name. With `NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES` set, `SELECT 'a\\b'` returns `a\b`. When the session `sql_mode` step fails, the query is not run.

Under a set that lists `customers` (`id`, `name`, `account_id`) and `orders` (`id`, `customer_id`, `total`), on tables that both have `account_id`, `SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE c.id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE account_id = 2)` runs with `account_id` resolved to `customers.account_id`. Part 1 adds no check for this beyond the prompt's guidance to qualify every column.

Under the example set, each of these is refused before execution, at minimum: `SELECT name FROM otherdb.customers`, `SHOW TABLES`, `DESCRIBE customers`, two statements in one call, a write statement with `database.read_only = false`, a read of `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.STATISTICS`, a read of `mysql.user`, a read from a view, a stored function call, `JSON_TABLE`, `FROM DUAL`, `SELECT name /*!50000 , email */ FROM customers` with `database.read_only = false`, `SELECT name INTO @v FROM customers`, `SELECT c.name FROM customers PARTITION (p1) c`, `SELECT c.name FROM customers c FORCE INDEX (PRIMARY)`, and SQL that sqlglot cannot parse.

Under the example set, `SELECT c.name FROM (customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.discount > 5)` fails with MySQL's unknown-column error, and the same statement without `AND o.discount > 5` returns rows. `SELECT /*+ BKA('*\/ email FROM customers -- ') */ name FROM customers` returns no value of `customers.email`.

Under the example set, `SELECT c.name, d.total FROM customers c JOIN LATERAL (SELECT o.total FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY o.total DESC LIMIT 1) d ON TRUE` runs and returns rows, while the same statement whose lateral body reads `o.discount` fails with MySQL's unknown-column error (1054) and returns no value of `orders.discount`.
The rule-set guard refuses every statement to which no row of the Desired Behavior's guard table gives an outcome.

Under the example set, a statement the rule-set guard cannot carry through is refused before execution, with no SQL reaching MySQL, at minimum in these cases: an exception raised in each of the guard's parse, analyze, rewrite and generate steps, including an exception type the guard does not name, and, with `database.refuse_whole_row_selects` set to false, a `run_sql` argument whose parse yields no statement (empty text and comment-only text). Each of those refusals' client-facing text begins with `Refused by the rule set:` and names no table, column or function.

Under the example set, with `database.refuse_whole_row_selects` left at its default of true, a `run_sql` argument whose parse yields no statement — empty text and comment-only text — is refused before execution with no SQL reaching MySQL, and the client-facing text names no table, column or function. The change leaves that case to the whole-row guard, so its text does not begin with `Refused by the rule set:`.
Under the example set, a read of `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES`, `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS` or `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.KEY_COLUMN_USAGE` is refused before execution.
With no `[[rls]]` rules and a rule-set file configured, a query that passes a listed column to a stored function the database defines is refused.

With a listed column dropped from the database after the existence check passed, a query that reads it fails with MySQL's unknown-column error, even inside a correlated subquery whose outer table has a column of the same name. A statement that reaches the rule-set guard for a request with no selected rule set is refused.

With a flat `[[rls]]` rule on `orders.account_id` (a column the example set does not list) and the example set selected, `SELECT o.total FROM orders o` runs and returns only rows that match the flat rule.

While a rule-set file is configured, the text returned for a refusal by the rule-set guard, the whole-row guard, flat RLS, the relation check, the function denylist or the read-only guard names no table, column or function (`SELECT email FROM customers WHERE`, which fails to parse, included, with `database.refuse_whole_row_selects` on and off), and every rule-set guard refusal begins with `Refused by the rule set:`.

While a rule-set file is configured, every refusal by the rule-set guard, the whole-row guard, flat `[[rls]]`, the relation check, the function denylist or the read-only guard writes one WARNING-level server log record carrying the full reason, including the table, column or function name the client-facing text omits, and no value returned to the client carries that detail.

While a rule-set file is configured, the system prompt's MySQL guidance tells the model to qualify every column with its table name or alias, and its Tool Errors section tells the model to correct and rerun a query whose `run_sql` error says `Refused by the rule set:` (the model sees it after the `Error executing query: ` prefix), within the two-attempt limit. The prompt differs from today's prompt for the same configuration with `memory.save_queries` and `memory.save_text_memories` off by those two changes only, so no rule set's `scope` or provenance reaches the model.
Without a rule-set file configured, the system prompt is byte-identical to today's for the same configuration.

While a rule-set file is configured, a conversation continues for requests with the identity that started it, a request presenting its `conversation_id` under another rule set, account ID or user ID is refused with `isError` before the agent runs, and the owner's next turn still sees the full history. This holds also for a request under another identity that arrives while the owner's first turn on that `conversation_id` is still running.
While a rule-set file is configured, the agent has neither `save_question_tool_args` nor `save_text_memory`, even with `memory.save_queries` and `memory.save_text_memories` on.
While a rule-set file is configured, `list_data_sources` answers a call that carries no `_meta`.
While a rule-set file is configured, `sqllens verify-memory` exits non-zero before running any case, with a message that it does not support rule sets yet.
Under a rule set, a request that names a profile whose `show_details` is on is served under the same rule-set guard: a query reading `customers.email` still fails as an unknown column.

With no rule-set file configured, a `query_database` request that runs today runs with the same result, no request is refused for missing rule-set `_meta`, and the agent's memory-write tools follow `memory.save_queries` and `memory.save_text_memories` as today.

The change leaves these unchanged, each as one unit: the rule-set file is read once at startup, so an edit made while the server runs changes nothing until restart; memory retrieval, which stays shared by every rule set; the memory-admin, `import_memory` and profile-admin tools, which keep acting on the shared store and profiles for every rule set; `/readyz`, which reports ready while the existence check fails; and the MCPB bundle manifest, which gains no entry for the rule-set file.

This issue adds nothing for these, each as one unit: MySQL syntax that sqlglot writes back in a form MySQL rejects (for example a bare `UTC_DATE`, which comes back as a quoted identifier, or `UTC_DATE()`, which comes back as `CURRENT_DATE AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'`) fails with MySQL's error; `CAST(x AS REAL)`, which sqlglot writes back as single-precision `CAST(x AS FLOAT)`, runs with less precision; a query without `ORDER BY` can return rows in the order of an index on a column the set does not list, which can reveal the order of that column's values; and MySQL's `derived_merge` optimizer switch, which SQL Lens neither checks nor sets, so a server with it off materializes each derived table the guard builds.
